interviewQuestions.question: Walk through the cache layers a single image request passes through in a well-built mobile app, and what each layer's job is.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A request checks in-memory cache first — fastest, but volatile and limited by available RAM, so it typically holds only recently-viewed content. A miss there checks disk cache — survives app restarts, much larger capacity, but genuinely slower than memory since it's real disk I/O. A miss there goes out over the network, ideally terminating at a geographically close CDN edge rather than crossing to the origin server directly. Only a miss at every layer actually reaches the origin, which is the slowest and most expensive path.

The part that's easy to get wrong isn't the check order, it's the **write-back** direction: when a slower layer produces a hit (disk, or a network fetch), the result should be promoted into the faster layers above it — a disk hit written into memory, a network fetch written into both disk and memory — so the *next* request for the same data climbs the hierarchy instead of repeating the same slow path every time. Skipping that promotion step is a common, subtle bug that quietly defeats a chunk of the caching strategy's benefit without causing an obvious failure.

I'd also note that correctness matters more than hit rate here — a fast cache that occasionally serves stale or wrong data is worse for the product than a slightly slower one that's reliably accurate, so I'd pick each layer's invalidation approach based on how much staleness the specific data can tolerate.

**Testing:** whether you understand both directions of the hierarchy — falling through on a miss, and promoting on a hit — not just the check order.

interviewQuestions.question: Design the caching and invalidation strategy for a grocery delivery app's product catalog, given that prices and stock levels change throughout the day.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd split this by field, not treat the whole product record as one cacheable unit with one strategy, because different fields have very different staleness tolerances. Product metadata — name, description, images — changes rarely, so a generous time-based TTL (hours, not seconds) is fine and keeps the app fast without meaningfully risking user-visible errors.

Price and stock level are the fields that actually matter for correctness here — showing a stale price a user then tries to check out with, or showing an item as in stock when it just sold out, produces real user-facing problems (a broken checkout, a canceled order after the fact) that are worse than a slightly slower screen. For these specific fields, I'd use server-driven revalidation on every screen visit at minimum — a lightweight endpoint the client checks before allowing checkout, even if the rest of the product page is served from cache — and if the product has capacity for it, push-invalidation for active carts specifically (notify a client whose cart contains an item that just went out of stock or changed price), since that's exactly the case where staleness has a real, immediate cost that justifies the added infrastructure.

I'd cache images aggressively with a long TTL and a bounded disk cache with LRU eviction, since images are large, expensive to re-fetch, and change essentially never once uploaded — the opposite profile from price/stock.

The overall principle I'd apply: derive the invalidation strategy per field from its actual real-world cost of being stale, not apply one blanket TTL to the whole product object.

**Testing:** whether you can differentiate invalidation strategy by data type within one entity, rather than treating a whole record as one cache unit.

interviewQuestions.question: Your app's feed screen prefetches the next page as the user scrolls, but users on a data-limited plan complain about excessive data usage. How would you fix this without giving up the smooth-scroll benefit entirely?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't disable prefetching outright — that gives up a real, meaningful UX win (no visible loading gap while scrolling) for users who don't have this specific problem, most of whom are on Wi-Fi or an unlimited plan. The actual mistake causing the complaint is treating every connection as equally cheap to speculate on, when metered cellular specifically isn't.

My fix: check the actual connection type before deciding how aggressively to prefetch. On Wi-Fi, prefetch generously — bandwidth is effectively free there, so the trade favors speculation heavily. On cellular, either throttle prefetch distance (fetch one page ahead instead of three) or disable it entirely by default, and respect any platform-level 'data saver' signal or an explicit in-app setting if the product wants to expose one.

I'd also reconsider what's actually being prefetched, not just when — if the feed's thumbnails are already reasonably sized, prefetching the next page's metadata and thumbnail URLs is cheap even on cellular; it's specifically prefetching full-resolution images or heavy payloads speculatively that's expensive and worth gating more conservatively.

I'd validate the fix with the same kind of before/after production metric discipline as any performance change — confirm data usage per session actually drops for cellular users after the change, not just assume the fix worked because it seems logically correct.

**Testing:** whether you can make a nuanced, connection-aware fix instead of the blunt 'turn the feature off' response to a complaint.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: A support ticket says a user saw an item as 'in stock' in the app, ordered it, and then got a cancellation email because it was actually out of stock. How would you investigate whether this is a caching bug?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My working hypothesis, given the specific symptom — stale data shown, then a real-world consequence from acting on it — is that the stock-level field is being served from a cache layer with an invalidation strategy that's too loose for how quickly stock actually changes, or the checkout flow isn't specifically revalidating stock at the moment of purchase.

I'd check the actual caching configuration for the stock field: what TTL is it using, and does the checkout screen re-fetch fresh stock data before confirming an order, or does it trust whatever was already cached from when the user first viewed the product? If checkout doesn't revalidate, that's the root cause regardless of what TTL is configured — the fix there is a mandatory fresh check (or at least a conditional revalidation) specifically at the point of commitment, not just anywhere earlier in the flow.

I'd also check whether this is a one-off (a specific race — someone else bought the last unit in the seconds between the user's view and their checkout, which no caching strategy fully eliminates) versus a systemic pattern (many tickets, suggesting the cache is stale for meaningfully longer than the checkout flow accounts for). The fix differs: a rare race might just need clearer post-purchase messaging and a smooth cancellation/refund flow, while a systemic staleness problem needs the caching strategy itself tightened for this specific field.

I'd push back on any fix that just shortens the TTL uniformly without addressing whether checkout revalidates at all — a five-minute-old cache is still capable of producing this exact ticket if checkout never double-checks before confirming.

**Testing:** whether you can distinguish a caching-strategy bug from a fundamental race condition, and know that checkout-time revalidation is the actual fix for the former.
